newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Air cargo ex-Ams rates to Asia due to rise in March.
newsitem.headline: Air cargo ex-Ams rates to Asia due to rise in March.

text.p: Heavy air cargo traffic in flowers for Valentine's Day was the key feature in a market awaiting rate increase to come into effect in March, a Reuters survey showed.

The boom in flower trade and talk of romance saw flowers being rushed into and out of the world's largest flower auction at Aalsmeer near Amsterdam in a last minute rush to have them ready available for Valentine Day's gifts.
This week, in Reuter's first ex-Amsterdam Asian/Middle East market report, talk otherwise centres very much on speculation of rates increases expected to be introduced in March.
Most carriers report that they have had a busy January despite it usually being a slow month. Chinese New Year does not seem to have slowed down trade too much, said several Reuter sources.

Cargo rates firmed up steadily. Hong Kong has increased from 2.80 guilders a kilo to 2.90 but they can reach as high as 3.10 guilders. Dutch national carrier, KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, started the ball rolling when it announced tariff increases effective March 1.

Rates for shipments from Amsterdam to the Middle East will increase by up to five percent and on Asia-Pacific the rates are set to increase by between five and ten percent. The national carrier also announced increases ranging from between 20 and 30 percent to the Indian Sub-Continent.
These rates rises are all independent of the 20 Dutch cents fuel surcharge introduced by KLM last year.

Traffic and capacity to and from the Asia Pacific market saw strong growth in the final part of last year, said KLM. But for the nine months ending December 31, traffic growth was strongest to and from the Middle East and South Asia which saw a rise of 20 percent, the carrier said in a statement.
For January, KLM said cargo traffic increased by one percent and this was coupled with a four percent decrease in capacity. The Dutch carrier is making efforts to reduce its capacity in the market.

Cargo capacity on routes to and from the Middle East and South Asia is more than ten percent less than in the same period in 1996, said the airline, which was largely a result of less leased-in capacity.
One area where KLM's efforts can be noted is in the Netherlands-India market and India is perhaps the destination causing the most interest at the moment.
KLM is initiating steep rates increases of 20 to 30 percent in rates and Lufthansa will also introduce similar rises in the Dutch- India market. Air India too, is also likely to follow.
It is widely acknowledged that rates to India need to go up, rates to Bombay are very low at 2.20-2.25 guilders a kilo.

KLM's bid to cut capacity can also be seen in this market. The carrier was leasing in a Boeing 747 freighter from Atlas Air which was often deployed on routes to India but the airline has cancelled this recently.
Cargo manager of Air India, Herman Eikema, said there is currently a severe capacity shortage in the Dutch-India market. Air India itself cancelled a Boeing 747 Combi three weeks ago.
Currently, Air India is trucking to Frankfurt and Paris where it operates 747 Combi services, said Eikema. "There is too much cargo, we like to say yes when we sell but there is not enough capacity."

Everything from electronic and spare parts to flower bulbs are being sent to India. The bulbs are sent to India where they are grown and then they are re-exported. Often these flowers are sent on to the Middle East.

The Indian market started to boom when India liberalised its air cargo market, he said. Import procedures have also been changed speeding up the whole process dramatically and import taxes have also been considerably reduced, he said, which has encouraged more trade.
The market is fairly busy at the moment because many Indian companies close their accounts in April and are importing goods before then, said one forwarder.
But just as some companies are withdrawing capacity from the Indian market, Polar Air is set to introduce a freighter service to the Middle East and India next week.

Other Asian destinations are also relatively busy. Achim van der Graaff, Cathay Pacific cargo manager, said January had proved a very good month for the Hong Kong-based carrier, with traffic up 20 percent and its daughter company Air Hong Kong had seen cargo volumes increase by 50 percent, he said.
However, Van der Graaff stressed that these steep January increases could be because the first few months of 1996 were quite slow in comparison to other years.
February was a little slower than expected, he added, but this was a time when aircraft tended to go in for maintenance.

Cathay Pacific will also be one of those carriers introducing rates increases ex-Amsterdam from March 1. Depending on destination, the increases will very from five to 15 Dutch cents. The airline implemented a ten Dutch cents increase in December last year, although it did not introduce a fuel surcharge like most carriers.
Japan is seeing a mini-boom currently. Japan Airlines cargo sales manager, Pim de Goederen, said JAL is one of the carriers hoping to benefit from expected VAT increases in Japan.
Many of those in the Netherlands-Japan trade have been hopeful that there would be a rush of cargo heading for Japan as VAT is expected to rise by three to five percent.
De Goederen said this has undoubtedly been a factor in Febuary, when more and more cargo heads for Japan before the April 1 VAT deadline.
JAL steered clear of a fuel surcharge last year but it did increase rates by two to five percent in January. And this will probably be followed by a similar increase in April.
A spokesman for all-cargo carrier, Nippon Cargo Airlines, said it too was experiencing more demand because of the VAT increase.
Rates have reflected the situation in the Japanese market, they have increased from 4.35 to 4.50 guilders.
Cargolux will also be introducing rates increases ex- Amsterdam, a spokesman said. These will be introduced on all routes and range from between five to seven percent, he added.
After a particularly busy Christmas period, where the lack of capacity was a major factor, the Middle East market seems to have calmed down. Rates have remained steady, with some increasing slightly.
Also as Ramadan comes to an end, carriers that had aircraft in for maintenance are expected to up their capacity again to usual levels.
Tijn Middendorp, MSAS Middle East director, said February has been a relatively successful month so far and he was optimistic about prospects for the next few weeks.

Strangely enough, a major export to the Middle East - Dutch eggs - are very much in demand at the moment. Hatching egggs are a major export from the Netherlands but a shortage has led the Dutch to import them from the U.S.. Prices have risen from ten cents an egg to 35 cents, said one source.

Currently those involved in the Dutch-Middle East, like those in the India market, are eyeing Polar Air, which is starting its twice-weekly Boeing 747 freighter service to Dubai and Delhi on February 17.
"It will be interesting to see what rates Polar Air brings to the market," said one source. -- Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+5017
